Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District EXECUTIVE SUMMARY [SOURCE: Page_5]

The Government of Bangladesh, through the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) under Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, Bangladesh, is implementing the “Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER)” Project with financial assistance from the World Bank. As part of the project’s disaster resilience strategy, 21 flood and disaster-resilient shelters are proposed for construction across two highly vulnerable upazilas of Bogura District -Gabtali (12 sites) and Shariakandi (9 sites). The proposed shelters are designed not only to provide safe refuge for local populations, livestock, and essential assets during flood emergencies, but also to function as community facilities such as schools or multipurpose centers during non-disaster periods, ensuring sustainable year-round utilization. The target upazilas in Bogura are located along the flood-prone Jamuna River and its adjoining floodplains, where communities are frequently exposed to seasonal flooding, riverbank erosion, and associated livelihood disruptions. The sites are located in low-lying flood-prone areas with recent alluvial soil, and fall under Seismic Zone II & III, indicating moderate earthquake vulnerability. These geological and topographical characteristics demand climate- and disaster- resilient designs, especially considering the district’s exposure to annual monsoon flooding and riverbank erosion. The proposed subproject comprises (i) construction of climate-resilient flood shelter; and (ii) construction and rehabilitation of connecting roads, including culverts and bridges. The overall anticipated adverse impact due to the subproject intervention is limited and site specific. Considering the environmental impact for construction of flood shelters construction and rehabilitation of connecting roads which is anticipated as insignificant; hence the overall project risk is categorized as Moderate, under the World Bank ESF. However, since none of the project components are listed under Schedule-1 of the Environmental Conservation Rules, 2023, the Department of Environment (DoE) has formally exempted the project from the requirement of obtaining an Environmental Clearance Certificate (ECC). [SOURCE: Page_5]

Environmetnal and Social Standard-1 (ESS$_1$) of ESF underscores the responsibility of assessing, managing, and monitoring environmental and social risks and impacts of projects/sub-projects through a risk- and outcome-based approach, ensuring sustainability and compliance with the Environmental and Social Standards (ESSs). The environmental and social assessment serves as a key instrument to inform project design, identify mitigation measures, and strengthen decision-making proportionate to the project’s level of risk. In line with these principles, the ES Team of the Design and Supervision (D&S) Consultant of the project conducted an in-depth environmental and social survey and Assessment from June 28 – July 06, 2025, across all 21 proposed sites in Bogura District, where school-cum-flood shelters with associated facilities, along with school connecting roads to several of these shelters, are planned for construction. [SOURCE: Page_5]

Page | v [SOURCE: Page_5]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District Upazila based ES findings with suggested ESMP and Site specific environmental and social description and assessment results as well as and its tentative implementing cost (BOQ) are presented in Annexure 1 and Asessment formats and consultation checklist are attached in Annexure 2 and Annexure 3 respectively. Attendance of the consultation meetings are in Annexure 4. All flood shelters are required to have minimum of 33 decimals of land; copies of land ownership documents of all shelters have been collected and verified. The project has no provision for land acquisition or compensation for land and property, as all planned activities will be implemented on existing or government-owned land. Access roads might need to be constructed or rehabilitated within its existing alignment. [SOURCE: Page_6]

According to the Land Readiness Status Report, a total of 20 out of 21 proposed multipurpose flood shelter sites (one site to be replaced) were found to be compliant with the project’s legal and policy frameworks and land selection criteria, demonstrating adequate land availability, clear ownership records, and no risk of involuntary resettlement or displacement. Among these compliant sites, 15 schools require demolition of existing old buildings, while 2 schools need demolition of existing wash blocks to make space for new construction. In addition, 8 of these schools where old structures will be demolished require temporary school sheds, as recommended by the School Management Committees (SMCs) to ensure uninterrupted education for students during the construction period. [SOURCE: Page_6]

However, one school in Shariakandi Upazila was identified as critical for decision making about the availability of land for construction works, as the SMC expressed a strong interest in preserving the existing playground, which had originally been proposed as the flood shelter site. Despite these challenges, five schools are fully ready for immediate construction without the need for demolition or major preparatory works. For all schools where site-related issues were raised, concerns have been resolved through consultations with the SMCs and local communities, followed by field verification of design alignment to ensure compliance with both technical and social requirements. [SOURCE: Page_6]

This Environmental and Social Assessment and Management Report (ESAMR) has been prepared in line with the requirements of the World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) and relevant national environmental regulations to identify, assess, and manage potential environmental and social risks associated with the shelter construction. The Assessment process included site visits, stakeholder consultations, environmental and social impact assessment and identification. Key anticipated environmental impacts include vegetation loss, dust and noise generation, traffic congestion, disposal of construction waste, and possible soil erosion, while social impacts may include temporary disruption to community services, demolition of old structures, loss of trees within school premises, parts of a few water bodies as ditches, ponds, depressions etc. being likely to be filled due to the construction of the flood shelters and minor risk of labor influx-related conflicts. [SOURCE: Page_6]

The ecological impact of the subproject has been assessed as low to moderate, with no ethnic communities residing within the catchment area and no involuntary resettlement or loss of [SOURCE: Page_6]

Page | vi [SOURCE: Page_6]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District common property resources anticipated. Minor, temporary impacts may occur where school playgrounds are partially affected during construction, limiting children’s access for a short period. However, teachers, parents, and community members expressed strong support during consultations, recognizing that the proposed school-cum-flood shelters will provide safer educational facilities and serve as vital refuge centers for people and livestock during flood events. To minimize disruption, School Management Committees (SMCs) will identify and facilitate alternative playgrounds for temporary use. [SOURCE: Page_7]

In 15 schools, demolition of old school buildings or wash blocks is required, which will be implemented by separate contractors under the Directorate of Primary Education (DPE). These works will follow a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to mitigate potential noise, dust, and safety hazards, while the main construction-related impacts will remain limited and manageable within the existing premises. Among these 15 schools set for demolition (full or partial), 8 Schools will require temporary schooling arrangement for unterrupted learning opportunities to pupils, which will be constructed by the construction contractor. [SOURCE: Page_7]

The construction contractor will use available school land for storage and work areas and obtain any additional temporary land through formal tenancy agreements. Site-specific Environmental and Social Management Plans (ESMPs) with tailored mitigation measures have been prepared for each Upazila to ensure compliance and minimize environmental and social risks. [SOURCE: Page_7]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 1     INTRODUCTION [SOURCE: Page_8]

1.1    Sub-project Background Flood is an integral part of Bangladesh and so is the suffering of the people living in flood-prone areas. Bangladesh is one of the most vulnerable countries to natural disasters including floods where almost every year, mainly during monsoon season, either by upstream river floods and or by heavy rainfall. During floods, people, their essential belongings and livestock in the affected areas need to take shelters for few days to as long as 8 weeks. Sometimes floods take considerable time to recede even 70 days as in 1998. But there is great insufficiency of flood resilient shelter including killas, raised public infrastructure for them to take shelter. People often took shelters in high embankment, schools and colleges in high land affecting their normal operation and spreading diseases among them and others. Unlike cyclone shelters, very few designated flood shelters exist in Bangladesh. [SOURCE: Page_8]

In the backdrop of people’s plight or sufferings, caused by recurring flood events and lightning, the Government of Bangladesh, with support from the World Bank, is implementing the “Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER)” Project, aimed at enhancing disaster resilience through the construction of Primary School Cum Multipurpose flood shelters and related infrastructure in disaster-prone regions. The project is being implemented by Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives (MoLGRDC), Bangladesh. As part of this project, a total of 21 multipurpose disaster shelters has been proposed for construction in Bogura district, distributed across two highly vulnerable upazilas as Gabtali (12 sites) and Shariakandi (9 sites). These upazilas are located along the Jamuna River and its tributaries, which are historically prone to seasonal floods, riverbank erosion, and other climate- induced hazards. Communities in these areas face recurring challenges, including displacement, damage to agricultural land and livelihoods, and loss of critical infrastructure. [SOURCE: Page_8]

The proposed shelters are designed to serve dual purposes: functioning as educational institutions during normal periods and as life-saving shelters during floods and other natural disasters. Facilities would include, climate resilient features comprising, sustainable water supply system, standby solar electrical system, assured water supply source, rainwater harvesting provisions, installation of lightning protection systems, and adequate health and hygiene systems. Facilities would also include provision for protection of livestock and adequate storage provisions. Associated management, operations and maintenance related issues would be addressed through strengthening the capacity of the associated SMC and UDMC, for effective disaster related adaptation, preparedness and response, among other interventions. [SOURCE: Page_8]

This Environmental and Social Assessment and Management Report (ESAMR) aims to assess the potential environmental and social impacts associated with the proposed sub-projects activities as tree cutting, land filling, demolition of old structures, increased dust and noise levels, traffic congestion, and temporary disruption of community services and to recommend suitable [SOURCE: Page_8]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District mitigation measures aligned with national regulatory frameworks and the World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF). The findings of this assessment will inform project design, implementation planning, and safeguard compliance to ensure that the shelters are constructed and operated in an environmentally sound, socially inclusive, and sustainable manner. [SOURCE: Page_9]

1.2   Objective of the Project [SOURCE: Page_9]

The objective of the project is to reduce the adverse impacts of floods and to provide safe spaces for evacuation and sheltering through the development of resilient infrastructure. The project also seeks to prevent long-term negative impacts of flooding and to enhance community resilience by strengthening local capacity for effective early warning, disaster preparedness, and emergency response. [SOURCE: Page_9]

Specifically, the project aims to: (a) Increase the number of people with reduced flood vulnerability through the establishment of climate-resilient and protective infrastructure; and (b) Enhance the disaster preparedness capacity of both the Government of Bangladesh (GoB) and local communities. In addition, the project contributes to the COVID-19 recovery process by supporting public works that generate local employment opportunities, thereby improving livelihood conditions in rural areas. [SOURCE: Page_9]

The project will finance infrastructure and systems that strengthen the flood resilience of vulnerable rural populations in selected areas by: (i) Raising community land, constructing multi- purpose flood shelters, community facilities, connecting roads, and other flood-resilient infrastructure in flood-prone villages; and (ii) Enhancing community disaster preparedness through improved early warning systems, evacuation planning, awareness and training programs, and strengthened response and recovery capacity. [SOURCE: Page_9]

1.3   Scope of the Project [SOURCE: Page_9]

The scope of the project shall include the construction of multipurpose flood shelters and construction of related access roads, flood embankments, drainage channels (both natural and manmade). The proposed infrastructure shall be climate resilient, including cross-drainage culverts and rural bridges necessary for assured rural accessibility. Raising of selected community land above the high flood level and small-scale community infrastructure to protect land and property shall also be included. 1.4   Objectives of the Report [SOURCE: Page_9]

The general objective of this study is to determine the major environmental and social impacts succeeding from construction and operation of the subproject and to recommend mitigation measures to avoid or reduce adverse environmental and social impacts and to enhance positive impacts. The specific objectives include: [SOURCE: Page_9]

Page | 2 [SOURCE: Page_9]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District     To assess the existing environmental and social conditions of the subproject site and its influence area;     To identify and assess impacts resulting from the subproject during its construction phase and operation phase;     To develop an environmental and social management plan (ESMP) with recommendations for mitigating impacts and enhance positive impacts;     To summarize environmental and social monitoring requirements. [SOURCE: Page_10]

The report focuses on site-specific characteristics of the proposed shelter locations within Bogura district, the sensitivity of the surrounding environment, and the socio-economic conditions of the target communities. It is intended to guide project developers, implementing agencies, and other stakeholders in making informed decisions that minimize negative impacts and enhance the positive outcomes of the RIVER project. [SOURCE: Page_10]

1.5       Institutional Arrangements 1.5.1 Implementing Agency for the Project The Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) will be responsible for implementing the project. LGED will implement the project through a dedicated Dhaka-based Project Implementation Unit (PIU), headed by a Project Director (PD). The PD is supported by a dedicated Deputy Project Director (DPD), Senior Assistant Engineer, Assistant Engineer as well as the associated technical and safeguard support staff. A majority of the implementation will be based on the district and Upazila levels, where the associated LGED field officials (i.e., Executive Engineer, Sr. Assistant Engineer, Assistant Engineer, Sub assistant Engineer etc.) will act as the focal person(s) responsible for supervision and monitoring of work implementation in their respective districts and Upazilas. [SOURCE: Page_10]

1.5.2 Project Implementation Unit The PIU would provide support to implement the ES instruments during implementation of the project. ## 3     BASELINE ANALYSIS OF THE ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIO-ECONOMIC CONDITION

3.1    Physical Environment 3.1.1 Geology, Topography, and Soils Geology Bogura district is situated within the floodplain region of the Brahmaputra–Jamuna River system, forming part of the Tista and Jamuna floodplains in northwestern Bangladesh. The geological formation is dominated by recent alluvial deposits of sand, silt, and clay, carried by the Jamuna, Karatoa, and Bangali rivers, with very limited tertiary deposits in the northern edges. Subsurface stratigraphy is characterized by unconsolidated sediments, which are highly suitable for agriculture but vulnerable to erosion, sedimentation, and seasonal flooding (BGS & DPHE, 2001). [SOURCE: Page_16]

Topography Topographically, the district is generally flat to gently undulating, with an average elevation ranging between 20–30 meters above mean sea level. The land is intersected by river channels, [SOURCE: Page_16]

Page | 9 [SOURCE: Page_16]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District natural depressions, and floodplain ridges, which influence local hydrology. Seasonal inundation is common, especially in the low-lying areas of Shariakandi and Gabtali upazilas along the Jamuna River, while the central and western parts are relatively higher and less flood-prone. Riverbank erosion along the Jamuna poses a continuous risk to settlements and agricultural land, contributing to land loss and displacement. [SOURCE: Page_17]

Soil Conditions Soil characteristics of Bogura district are primarily non-calcareous alluvium, with variations across different floodplain units. The dominant soils include clay loam, silty clay, and sandy loam, which are fertile and support intensive cultivation of rice, jute, wheat, and vegetables. However, the soils are prone to seasonal waterlogging in depressions and low-lying floodplains. In some areas, light-textured sandy soils are present, particularly near riverine char lands, which are less fertile and more vulnerable to drought stress. Overall, the soil resources of Bogura are highly productive but require effective water and erosion management for sustainable use (SRDI, 2018). [SOURCE: Page_17]

According to the Seismic Zoning Map of BNBC 2015, Bangladesh comprises four seismic zones, where Bogura District falls under Seismic Zone II and III and the Seismic Coefficient value is 0.20 to 0.28g as per the Bangladesh National Building Code (BNBC 2015), indicating a moderate seismic risk. Although not located in the most seismically active zone of the country, the region is susceptible to moderate-intensity earthquakes, typically ranging from 5.0 to 6.0 on the Richter scale. Historical records and geological assessments indicate that while large-magnitude earthquakes are infrequent in this area, low to moderate tremors occur occasionally, especially as a result of tectonic activity along the Madhupur Fault and distant Himalayan seismic sources. Considering this, all proposed infrastructure such as flood shelters under the RIVER Project must comply with earthquake-resilient design standards outlined in BNBC to ensure structural safety and disaster resilience. Refer to Figure 3.1 for the earthquake zone map, showing Bogura district. [SOURCE: Page_17]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 3.1.2 Climate and Meteorology Bogura district falls under the tropical monsoon climate zone of Bangladesh, characterized by hot summers, heavy monsoon rainfall, and mild, dry winters. The climate is largely influenced by the southwest monsoon winds, which bring the majority of annual precipitation, and the retreating northeast monsoon during the dry season. The average annual rainfall in Bogura ranges from 1,800 to 2,200 mm, with nearly 80% concentrated between June and September (BMD, 2022). The monsoon season is often marked by intense rainfall events, causing flash floods and waterlogging in low-lying areas, particularly in Shariakandi and Gabtali upazilas located along the Jamuna floodplain. In contrast, the dry season (November–March) experiences very low rainfall, often below 50 mm per month, leading to moisture stress in agriculture without irrigation support. The temperature regime is typical of northwestern Bangladesh, with mean maximum temperatures ranging from 32–36°C in April–June (pre-monsoon summer), while mean minimum temperatures drop to 10–12°C in January (winter). High humidity levels prevail during the monsoon (75–85%), whereas the dry season is relatively less humid. Climatic extremes such as heat waves, cold waves, and nor’westers (Kalbaishakhi storms) are common in Bogura. Heat waves in April–May frequently affect agriculture and human health, while cold waves during December–January particularly impact vulnerable populations such as children and the elderly. Seasonal fog events during winter also reduce visibility, disrupting road and air transport. Long-term climate observations indicate that the district is highly vulnerable to climate variability and change, with increasing trends in erratic rainfall, prolonged flooding, and higher intensity of extreme weather events (MoEFCC, 2018). These climatic conditions make the construction of flood-resilient infrastructure, such as multipurpose disaster shelters under the RIVER Project, crucial for safeguarding lives and livelihoods. Refers to Figure 3.2 for the Trend of annual average maximum temperature of North-Western district of Bangladesh. [SOURCE: Page_19]

Figure 3.2: Trend of annual average maximum temperature [SOURCE: Page_19]

Page | 12 [SOURCE: Page_19]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 3.1.3 Hydrology (Surface water, Ground water and Rain water) Bogura district lies within the Brahmaputra–Jamuna River basin, and its hydrology is dominated by an extensive network of rivers, floodplains, and wetlands. The major rivers include the Jamuna, Bangali, Karatoa, and Nagar, which together form the backbone of surface water resources in the district. Seasonal flooding of the Jamuna and its distributaries deposits fertile silt on floodplains, supporting intensive agriculture but also causing erosion and displacement in riparian areas, especially in Shariakandi and Gabtali upazilas. Numerous beels (natural depressions), ditches, and irrigation canals act as seasonal storage basins, providing water for irrigation, fisheries, and domestic use, but they are highly dependent on rainfall variability. Groundwater is the primary source of drinking water and irrigation in Bogura. Shallow tube wells (STWs) and deep tube wells (DTWs) are widely used for domestic and agricultural purposes. According to BGS & DPHE (2001), groundwater availability in Bogura is generally abundant, but some areas show seasonal depletion due to over-extraction for boro rice cultivation during the dry season. While the aquifers are relatively safe from salinity intrusion, iron and arsenic contamination have been reported in isolated pockets, though the problem is less severe compared to southern Bangladesh. Sustainable abstraction and regular quality monitoring are therefore essential to maintain groundwater security. Rainwater contributes significantly to the district’s hydrology, with an average annual rainfall of 1,800–2,200 mm, most of which occurs between June and September (BMD, 2022). This rainfall directly recharges surface water bodies and shallow aquifers. However, the uneven seasonal distribution results in water scarcity during the dry months (November–March), requiring heavy reliance on groundwater for irrigation. In contrast, intense monsoon rainfall often leads to waterlogging and drainage congestion in low-lying areas, exacerbating flood risks. Overall, the hydrological setting of Bogura reflects a dual challenge of seasonal flooding and dry- season water stress, making integrated water resource management and climate-resilient infrastructure crucial. The proposed flood shelters under the RIVER Project are therefore strategically important, as they will not only provide safe refuge during hydrological extremes but also ensure reliable water supply and sanitation facilities for affected communities. Refer to Figure 3.3 for the annual average rainfall of North-Western district of Bangladesh. [SOURCE: Page_20]

3.1.4 Flooding, Water Logging and Drainage Bogura district is situated on the floodplains of the Jamuna and Bangali rivers, making it highly susceptible to seasonal flooding and waterlogging. The most flood-prone upazilas are Shariakandi and Gabtali, located along the eastern boundary of the district, where the Jamuna River frequently overflows during the monsoon season (June–September). Historical records indicate that major floods in 1988, 1998, 2004, and 2017 inundated large parts of the district, damaging crops, settlements, schools, and road networks (BWDB, 2019). Seasonal floods deposit nutrient-rich silt that enhances soil fertility, but they also cause widespread loss of livelihoods, displacement, and erosion of riverbanks. Refer to Figure 3.4 for the flood zone areas of Bangladesh, with Bogura district within the low and moderate river flooding zone area. Waterlogging is a recurring problem in the low-lying floodplain depressions (beels and khals) of Bogura, particularly in areas where natural drainage is obstructed by embankments, unplanned road construction, and siltation of canals. During heavy monsoon rainfall, these areas remain submerged for weeks, disrupting agricultural activities and affecting homesteads. In contrast, during the dry season, many of these depressions dry up, highlighting the seasonal duality of water stress and water surplus in the district. Drainage in Bogura largely depends on natural river channels and floodplain connectivity. However, progressive siltation of rivers and khals, unplanned encroachment, and inadequate maintenance of drainage canals have significantly reduced drainage efficiency (WARPO, 2018). In Shariakandi, poor drainage capacity often leads to stagnant water, which exacerbates health risks such as mosquito breeding and waterborne diseases. To address these challenges, several flood control and drainage improvement schemes have been implemented by the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), including embankments and regulators along the Jamuna. Despite these interventions, the district remains highly vulnerable to climate-induced extreme rainfall and river flooding, making flood shelters and resilient infrastructure crucial for community safety. [SOURCE: Page_21]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 3.1.5 Air Quality and Dust The air quality of Bogura district reflects a combination of urban emissions, rural agricultural activities, and seasonal variations. In rural upazilas such as Gabtali and Shariakandi, ambient air quality is generally better than in urban centers, but it deteriorates during the dry season due to road dust, brick kiln emissions, biomass burning, and agricultural residue burning. According to the Department of Environment (DoE, 2022), the average concentration of particulate matter (PM10 and PM$_2$.5) in Bogura exceeds the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline values during the winter months, largely due to the operation of traditional brick kilns and transboundary pollution from surrounding districts. Brick kilns located along the Jamuna floodplain are major contributors to air pollution, emitting sulfur dioxide (SO₂), nitrogen oxides (NOx), and carbon monoxide (CO), in addition to suspended particulate matter. Dust generation is particularly high along unpaved rural roads, construction sites, and riverbank erosion-prone areas, where soil particles are exposed to wind during the dry months (December-March). During monsoon, however, dust levels decrease significantly due to rainfall and higher relative humidity. Local communities often report respiratory discomfort, eye irritation, and asthma complications during peak dust periods, especially among children and elderly people (DGHS, 2020). Although industrial activity in Bogura is limited compared to large cities, emissions from small- scale rice mills, vehicles, and brickfields collectively affect local air quality. Continuous urban expansion and construction works are also increasing dust and vehicular emissions in peri-urban areas. Overall, while the baseline air quality in Bogura is moderate compared to industrial zones like Dhaka or Gazipur, it shows clear evidence of seasonal dust pollution and particulate matter exceedances. This underscores the need for dust suppression measures, proper construction management, and regulatory monitoring during implementation of flood shelter projects to prevent localized air quality deterioration. To mitigate dust and air quality impacts, the ESSR recommends adopting best practices, including regular water sprinkling, covering of construction materials, vehicular emission control, and limiting vehicle speeds near sensitive receptors such as schools and homes are included ESMP. These measures will help maintain acceptable air quality during the shelter construction under the RIVER Project. [SOURCE: Page_23]

3.1.6 Noise Level The noise environment in Bogura district is influenced by both urban and rural sound sources, with notable variations between the municipal and upazila areas. In Bogura Sadar and surrounding urban centers, noise levels are predominantly generated from vehicular traffic, roadside markets, construction activities, workshops, and small-scale industries. According to the Department of Environment (DoE, 2022), daytime noise levels in Bogura Sadar often exceed the national permissible limit of 65 dB(A) for mixed areas, particularly along major transport corridors such as the Dhaka–Rangpur highway and the regional roads connecting Shariakandi, [SOURCE: Page_23]

Page | 16 [SOURCE: Page_23]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District Sherpur, and Shibganj. At night, although traffic reduces, roadside activities, local transport (three-wheelers, motorcycles), and goods movement still contribute to elevated noise levels. In semi-urban and rural upazilas, ambient noise levels are relatively lower and mainly associated with agricultural machinery (pumps, power tillers, threshers), riverine transport, and community activities. Seasonal construction of embankments, flood protection structures, and road development projects also cause temporary noise increases. During the harvesting season, widespread use of power tillers and rice mills can generate localized noise pollution, which affects nearby settlements. Excessive exposure to high noise levels in urban Bogura has been linked to stress, sleep disturbance, and hearing discomfort, especially among school children and elderly residents (DGHS, 2020). Noise pollution also affects sensitive institutions such as schools, mosques, and health centers located near busy transport routes. Overall, the baseline noise condition in Bogura reveals that urban areas face persistent noise exceedances compared to rural areas, where noise is mostly seasonal and activity-driven. For flood shelter construction, potential noise impacts will need to be carefully managed through the use of low-noise machinery, restricted working hours near sensitive receptors, and enforcement of DoE noise standards. [SOURCE: Page_24]

3.1.7 Solid Waste Management Solid waste management in Bogura district, including the sub-project upazilas Gabtali and Shariakandi, is characterized by limited formal collection systems and a strong reliance on community-based or household-level disposal practices. In Bogura municipal areas, waste is primarily managed by the Pourashava authority, which collects household waste from designated bins or roadside dumps and transports it to municipal disposal sites. However, coverage is far from universal, and a significant portion of the population resorts to open dumping in low-lying areas, roadside pits, water bodies, or agricultural land. A study by Waste Concern (2020) reported that nearly 70–75% of municipal waste in Bogura is organic in nature, originating from households, markets, and food processing units, while the remainder consists of plastics, metals, construction debris, and hazardous medical waste. In the rural areas of Gabtali and Shariakandi upazilas, where the RIVER project sub-project sites are located, waste management practices are even less structured. Most households manage their waste independently, often by open burning, composting organic waste for agricultural use, or indiscriminate disposal in nearby ditches, ponds, and riverbanks. This practice leads to localized water pollution, soil contamination, and health risks from vector-borne diseases. Plastic and polythene waste are of particular concern in rural bazaars, where they accumulate in drainage channels, creating blockages that worsen waterlogging during monsoon and flood events. During construction of flood shelters, construction debris, packaging materials, and excavated soil will add to the existing burden of unmanaged solid waste unless site-specific management [SOURCE: Page_24]

Page | 17 [SOURCE: Page_24]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District measures are implemented. Without proper handling, these materials could cause drainage obstruction, dust generation, and land degradation at the sub-project sites. To address these challenges, the Government of Bangladesh has adopted the Solid Waste Management Rules (2021), which emphasize segregation at source, recycling, and environmentally sound disposal. However, enforcement remains weak at the upazila level. Integrating project-level solid waste management into the flood shelter construction process— such as on-site segregation, composting of biodegradable waste, recycling of construction materials, and safe disposal of non-recyclables—is essential to align with both national regulations and World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESS$_3$: Resource Efficiency and Pollution Prevention and Management). [SOURCE: Page_25]

3.2   Biotic Environment as Floral and Faunal Existences The biotic environment of Bogura district is shaped by its fertile floodplains, riverine ecosystems, and agricultural landscapes, which together support a diverse range of flora and fauna. The district lies within the Barind Tract and floodplain ecological zones, where natural vegetation has been extensively modified due to agricultural expansion, settlement growth, and infrastructure development. Nevertheless, homestead forests, roadside plantations, wetlands, and riverbanks continue to provide habitats for important plant and animal species. The floral diversity of Bogura is dominated by cultivated crops such as rice, jute, wheat, mustard, maize, and vegetables, while homestead plantations include fruit trees (mango, jackfruit, banana, litchi, guava), timber species (mahogany, rain tree, sissoo, neem), and bamboo groves, which are common in rural households. Wetlands, canals, and rivers also sustain aquatic and semi-aquatic plants, including water hyacinth, lotus, reeds etc., which play an ecological role in nutrient cycling and as shelter for aquatic organisms. The faunal diversity of Bogura district includes a mix of domesticated, terrestrial, and aquatic species. Common terrestrial fauna includes small mammals (mongoose, jackal, fishing cat), rodents, and a wide variety of avian species, such as herons, egrets, storks, doves, mynas, and migratory waterfowl that use the floodplains and haor-like depressions as seasonal habitats. Amphibians and reptiles, including frogs, garden lizards, and water snakes, are also frequently observed in the rural wetlands. The aquatic ecosystems of the Jamuna, Bangali, and Karatoa rivers, along with numerous beels and ponds, provide habitats for diverse fish species, including carp, catfish, snakehead, and indigenous small fish, which are central to the district’s local nutrition and livelihoods. However, overfishing, pollution, and siltation have significantly reduced natural fish populations. Biodiversity in Bogura faces threats from deforestation of homestead forests, conversion of wetlands into cropland, unregulated fishing, and pollution from agriculture and domestic sources. Seasonal flooding, while beneficial to fish migration, also alters habitats, sometimes leading to the displacement of terrestrial fauna. No officially designated protected areas, wildlife sanctuaries, or ecologically critical areas (ECAs) are reported within the immediate project [SOURCE: Page_25]

Page | 18 [SOURCE: Page_25]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District influence zone, but the cumulative ecological functions of wetlands and riverine habitats are locally significant. For the flood shelter sub-project sites under the RIVER Project, potential impacts include tree cutting, disturbance to local fauna, and loss of vegetation in depressions or water bodies filled for construction purposes. Appropriate Environmental and Social Management Plans (ESMPs), including compensatory plantation, protection of wetland habitats, and awareness campaigns on biodiversity conservation will be necessary to minimize ecological impacts. [SOURCE: Page_26]

3.3   Socio-economic and Socio-cultural Environment [SOURCE: Page_26]

3.3.1 Land Use, Status of Housing and Built-up Infrastructure The land use pattern of Bogura District is predominantly agricultural, with cultivation of paddy, jute, wheat, maize, vegetables, and pulses occupying the majority of land (BBS, 2022). The district lies within the floodplains of the Jamuna and Karatoa rivers, with fertile alluvial soils that support multiple cropping cycles, while certain upazilas such as Shariakandi, Gabtali, Sonatala, and Dhunat are characterized by seasonally flooded lowlands, riverine chars, and wetlands that influence agricultural intensity and fisheries. Over the last three decades, built-up areas have expanded significantly, with remote sensing studies showing settlement areas increasing more than tenfold, while cultivable land has declined moderately and water bodies have decreased due to siltation and land conversion (BBS, 2022; BanglaJOL, 2023). Rural settlements are typically clustered homesteads built on raised earthen plinths, surrounded by trees, ponds, and cropland, whereas semi-urban and urban centers—particularly Bogura Sadar and its adjoining areas— feature brick-built houses, commercial establishments, educational institutions, health facilities, and government offices. Despite improvements, many rural households, especially in low-lying or flood-prone chars, still rely on tin-shed or thatched structures with inadequate sanitation and drainage. Infrastructure development has been notable, with the expansion of paved rural roads, bridges, culverts, flood control embankments, and multipurpose cyclone/flood shelters under LGED and BWDB projects, as well as national highways such as N502 and N510 enhancing regional connectivity. However, recurrent flooding and erosion continue to threaten rural infrastructure, prompting repeated rehabilitation efforts. Future development of flood shelters and public facilities in Bogura must align with existing land use patterns by minimizing the loss of cultivable land, ensuring resilient construction on elevated sites, and integrating water, sanitation, electricity, and communication networks to maximize community benefit during both normal and disaster periods. [SOURCE: Page_26]

3.3.2 Beneficiary Population The beneficiary population for flood-resilient shelters in rural communities of Bogura District includes vulnerable households—especially low-income families, women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities—who are disproportionately affected by seasonal flooding and disaster-related disruptions. According to the 2022 census, Bogra (Bogura) District is home to approximately 3.73 million people, with around 956,000 individuals aged 0–14 and 246,000 aged 65 and above, indicating a substantial youth and elderly population likely to require special [SOURCE: Page_26]

Page | 19 [SOURCE: Page_26]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District support in emergencies. While no official data isolates the count of low-income or disabled households at the district level, studies on char communities in Bogura reveal that flooding severely impacts rural poor, leading to significant income loss, degradation of agricultural livelihoods (affecting 54 % of households), property damage, health risks such as widespread diarrhea (76 % reported cases), and limited capacity for recovery due to depleted resources. These shelters are intended to offer safe refuge during disasters, protect lives, reduce displacement, and provide thousands of residents in flood-prone areas with emergency shelter and basic amenities, bolstering community resilience. Priority must be given to marginalized groups with limited resources to withstand recurring floods, ensuring that design, location, and access reflect equity and inclusion. [SOURCE: Page_27]

3.3.3 Tribal Communities According to the Bangladesh Population and Housing Census 2022 and anthropological records, Bogura District is not known to have any significant concentration of Indigenous Peoples (IPs) or tribal communities such as Santals, Oraons, Mundas, or Chakmas. The population is overwhelmingly Bengali Muslims and Hindus, with only a very small number of ethnic minority households—around 5,994 persons out of 3.73 million-reported as “ethnic population” in the census (BBS, 2022; Wikipedia, 2024). These families are mostly scattered across urban and peri- urban areas for employment, education, or occupational reasons, and they do not form socially cohesive or distinct ethnic communities, nor do they reside in traditional tribal settlements. The Environmental and Social Screening confirms that none of the proposed sub-project sites in Bogura’s rural upazilas fall within or near any recognized Indigenous Peoples’ settlements. Field verification and consultations with Union Parishads, school authorities, and community representatives also validated that no tribal households are located within the identified project influence zones. [SOURCE: Page_27]

In line with the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Framework (ESF), particularly Environmental and Social Standard (ESS) 7, a due diligence assessment has been carried out. Nevertheless, the project remains committed to inclusive stakeholder engagement, universal access, and equitable benefit-sharing for all vulnerable groups, ensuring that no segment of the population is excluded or adversely affected. [SOURCE: Page_27]

3.3.4 Land Acquisition The proposed flood shelter construction sub-projects under the RIVER Project in Bogura District do not require any private land acquisition. All identified sites across selected upazilas are situated within the premises of existing educational institutions, primarily government primary schools. The designated land is publicly owned, under the administrative authority of the respective school management committees and the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education (MoPME), and is therefore available for project use without legal complications (BBS, 2022; Wikipedia, 2024). Each shelter design has been developed through site-specific spatial assessments to ensure that construction activities remain fully contained within the existing school compound. There are no [SOURCE: Page_27]

Page | 20 [SOURCE: Page_27]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District residential or commercial structures, informal settlements, or agricultural activities on the proposed plots, eliminating the risk of involuntary resettlement or disruption of livelihoods in accordance with the World Bank’s ESS$_5$: Land Acquisition, Restrictions on Land Use, and Involuntary Resettlement. Field verification and consultations with Union Parishads, school authorities, and local communities in Bogura confirmed broad consent and cooperation from relevant stakeholders. The decision to use existing school land not only avoids land-related social risks but also ensures stronger integration of the flood shelters with local educational infrastructure, allowing for dual functionality—as educational facilities in normal times and as safe shelters during disaster events. [SOURCE: Page_28]

3.3.5 Land Readiness Status in Bogura District [SOURCE: Page_28]

A total of 20 (one site to be replaced) proposed multipurpose flood shelter construction sites out of the 21 sites were found to be compliant with the legal and policy frameworks as well as land selection criteria of the project, demonstrating sufficient land availability, clear ownership records, and no risk of involuntary resettlement or displacement. Within these compliant sites, 15 schools require demolition of existing old building where 2 schools need demolition of wash blocks to make space for the construction while 8 schools from these demolished sites needed temporary school shed since SMC proposed for the continuity of the education for the students. However, one school in Shariakandi upazila was identified as non-constructable due to SMC expressed a strong interest in preserving the existing playground which had been proposed as the site for the multipurpose flood shelter. Regardless of these challenges 5 schools are fully prepared for immediate construction without the need for demolition or major preparatory work. For all schools where issues were raised are addressed through proper consultation with SMC and local community and verifying design alignment in the field. [SOURCE: Page_28]

By ensuring the implementation of Environmental and Social Standards (ESS) and responsible land management options, the RIVER project will significantly contribute to enhancing disaster resilience and sustainable development in the flood-prone areas of Bogura district. Khatian or Deeds are included in Annexure-2 of the “Land Readiness Status Report of Bogura District” and most of the attained documents have been checked by effective website like https://dlrms.land.gov.bd/. [SOURCE: Page_28]

3.3.6 Principal Livelihoods and Economic Activities The economy of Bogura District is rooted in agriculture but has diversified into commerce, services, manufacturing, and remittances. Key sources of livelihood include:    Agriculture and Horticulture [SOURCE: Page_28]

Roughly 45 % of the workforce is engaged in agriculture, with fertile alluvial lands supporting crops like paddy and cash and minor crops—such as vegetables—growing in [SOURCE: Page_28]

Page | 21 [SOURCE: Page_28]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District char areas of Shariakandi, Sonatola, and Dhunot Upazilas In particular, organic vegetable cultivation, including chili and gourds, is gaining momentum in char regions [SOURCE: Page_29]

   Commerce, Services, and Small-scale Industry Commerce accounts for about 20.3 % of employment, with the service sector contributing another 16.2 % The district hosts over 4,000 small and medium enterprises in industries like food processing, plastics, textiles, engineering, and more. Many of these export goods across the region and internationally.    Non-farm Economic Engagement Additional livelihoods include transport and communication (8.5 %), construction (2.9 %), non-agricultural labor (2.8 %), and income from rent and remittances (0.7 %).    Livestock, Poultry, and Food Processing While specific figures for Bogura aren’t available, the Rural Development Academy, located in Sherpur Upazila, carries out research and outreach in livestock, poultry, pisciculture, and horticulture—suggesting local importance of these sectors. Notably, “Curd of Bogra” (Bogura) is a famous regional product, with thousands employed in its production facilities, particularly in yogurt making—a local specialty recognized for its unique quality.    Value Addition through Social Forestry Community-based forest initiatives (social forestry) have contributed to rural livelihoods by supplying fuelwood, fodder, and timber, while encouraging environmental awareness and offering economic support for poorer households. The flood shelter sub-projects are expected to have minimal impact on local livelihoods, as they will be built within existing school compounds. This approach avoids disruption to agricultural, commercial, or informal economic zones and aligns with resilience and continuity of community livelihoods. [SOURCE: Page_29]

3.3.7 Cultural Heritage and Protected Areas Bogura District has a deep cultural and historical legacy, often referred to as the “gateway to North Bengal” and home to several sites of national importance. Among the most notable are the Mahasthangarh archaeologica site, one of the earliest urban archaeological remains in Bangladesh, dating back to at least the 3rd century BCE, and recognized as a protected site by the Department of Archaeology. Other significant cultural landmarks include Behula Lakshindar Basor Ghar, linked with Bengali folklore; the Gokul Medh (Lakshindar Medh) Buddhist stupa; and several ancient mosques and Hindu temples scattered across the district. Bogura is also famous for its traditional dairy culture, particularly the production of “Curd of Bogura” (Bogurar Doi), which has become an iconic intangible cultural heritage of the region. There are no officially declared Ecologically Critical Areas (ECAs) or additional protected monuments situated near the proposed flood shelter sub-project sites under the RIVER Project. [SOURCE: Page_29]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District All shelters are planned within existing government primary school premises in populated rural settlements, ensuring that construction activities will not disturb any archaeological remains, cultural heritage sites, religious establishments, or historically significant structures. Standard mitigation measures will be applied during construction in accordance with the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) to safeguard both tangible and intangible cultural values of the local communities. [SOURCE: Page_30]

3.3.8 Social Conflicts and Development Activities The sub-project area is generally peaceful, and the local population is cooperative and supportive of development initiatives. Various government and non-government development programs, including infrastructure, education, and disaster resilience projects, have been successfully implemented in this district. The proposed flood shelter construction project is expected to receive positive acceptance from the community, as it directly addresses the pressing need for disaster preparedness and safety. During project implementation, no social conflicts are anticipated, and the project activities are unlikely to disrupt the existing social harmony. The construction sites have been selected in consultation with SMC, local stakeholders to ensure community ownership and minimal social risk. Proper Grievance Redress Mechanisms (GRM) should also be established to address community concerns transparently. [SOURCE: Page_30]

4   ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL SCREENING An Environmental and Social Screening was conducted for the proposed flood shelter subprojects under the “Resilient Infrastructure for Adaption and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER)” Project in Bogura district. The screening was carried out in accordance with the World Bank’s prescribed Screening Checklist (Annexure-2: Screening Checklist of Environmental and Social Safeguards) as outlined in the Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) of the project. The screening data and information for the proposed subprojects of Bogura district have been formulated and are shown in Annexure-1. The safeguard screening activities took place during June 28 – July 06, 2025, covering all proposed sites across the selected upazilas within the district. The objective of the screening was to identify potential environmental and social risks and impacts associated with the construction and operation of the flood shelters, and to propose appropriate mitigation and management measures. This report contains Upazila based ES findings with suggested ESMP and site-specific (individual report on each site) environmental and social screening findings of all the sub- projects under Bogura District, which are included in Annexure-1. The screening process involved site visits, stakeholder consultations (Annexure-3 gives the Consultation Meeting Checklist), review of environmental baselines, and assessment of social context including land use, vulnerable groups, and community dynamics. Based on the findings, an overall Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) has been developed for the subproject, outlining specific measures to mitigate adverse impacts during pre-construction, construction, and operational phases. [SOURCE: Page_30]

Page | 23 [SOURCE: Page_30]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District The ESMP includes provisions for waste management, dust and noise control, community health and safety, labor influx management, and grievance redress mechanisms. In addition, the plan emphasizes community consultations, Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM), and capacity building for local stakeholders. Regular environmental and social monitoring will be undertaken throughout the subproject lifecycle to ensure compliance with World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESSs) and national environmental regulations. [SOURCE: Page_31]

4.1   Summary of Environmental and Social Impacts [SOURCE: Page_31]

The construction of flood shelters in 21 sites of Bogura District involves diverse activities such as site clearing, excavation, material storage, transportation, and structural works, each of which can generate specific environmental and social impacts if not carefully managed. The environmental and social impacts anticipated from the proposed activities are generally minor to moderate in nature and largely site-specific, with no irreversible or long-term adverse effects expected. During the site preparation phase, clearing and dismantling of existing structures in 15 School Sites (by a third-party contractor) may lead to vegetation loss, dust and noise emissions, soil erosion, and temporary disruption to community movement. Earthworks in 3 specific sites, though in smaller scale, including cutting and filling may alter natural drainage patterns and increase the risk of sedimentation in nearby water bodies. The project’s ecological footprint is significant given its proximity to agricultural fields, homesteads, wetlands, and riverbanks. Improper storage of construction materials such as sand, cement, aggregates, and fuels can also lead to pollution of soil, air, and water, while accidental spillages may contaminate nearby ponds, canals, or agricultural lands. Water resources may also be at risk due to uncontrolled runoff, improper wastewater disposal, or leakage of hazardous substances. Given the flood-prone nature of the sites, construction runoff could lead to increased turbidity, sedimentation, and ecological stress in nearby rivers and wetlands. Air quality degradation and dust generation from excavation, material handling, and movement of construction vehicles are among the most common site-level impacts, often affecting sensitive receptors such as schools, clinics, mosques/ temple and residential areas. Noise and vibration from heavy equipment, pile driving, and demolition works can disturb community life, cause stress, and potentially damage weak structures. In addition, the project poses occupational health and safety (OHS) risks for workers due to physical hazards, heavy machinery operation, and exposure to dust, heat, and noise. Insufficient use of personal protective equipment (PPE) or poor site management may lead to accidents and injuries. Traffic congestion and community safety concerns may arise from increased vehicular movement, particularly on narrow rural roads shared by pedestrians and non-motorized transport. Potential grievances from nearby residents may arise if construction activities are not well-managed. [SOURCE: Page_31]

Page | 24 [SOURCE: Page_31]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District Overall, while the anticipated impacts are temporary and localized, they require systematic prevention, mitigation, and monitoring to protect both the surrounding environment and the wellbeing of workers and local communities. Apart from the overall impacts presented, some of the site-specific impacts have been revealed as well. For example, Tree removal is required in 16 sites, while temporary school is required to construct in 8 different sites. BOG-020 site is apprered to be critical in terms of availability of land, which requires rigoruous communication with the SMC and local inhabitatns. [SOURCE: Page_32]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 4.2   Overall Mitigation and Management Measures [SOURCE: Page_43]

To address the overall as well as site-specific risks, impacts or challenges, a set of integrated environmental and social management measures consistent with the Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP), Environmental and Social Codes of Practice (ESCOPs), and relevant Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been planned to follow at all working sites. [SOURCE: Page_43]

During site preparation and earthworks, dust suppression through regular watering, restriction of noisy operations to daytime hours, and controlled clearing of vegetation are prioritized. Fertile topsoil is to be stripped, stored, and reused for site landscaping or greenbelt development, while excavated slopes are stabilized immediately with silt fencing or sediment traps to prevent erosion. To minimize ecological disturbance, pre-construction ecological screening will identify sensitive habitats, and native trees and shrubs will be replanted after construction. Workers will receive orientation on eco-sensitive behavior, including the prohibition of waste dumping, wildlife disturbance, and fuel spillage. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Pollution prevention and material management will be ensured through designated storage areas with impermeable flooring and roofing, proper containment for fuels and chemicals, and housekeeping measures to prevent leaks and dust emissions. Sand and aggregate stockpiles will be covered, and construction vehicles will be maintained in good condition to reduce emissions. Air quality and noise management will include use of covered trucks, regular vehicle maintenance, temporary noise barriers near schools or health centers, and scheduling of pile driving or demolition works during off-peak hours. Noise and vibration levels will be periodically monitored to remain within the permissible limits of the Department of Environment (DoE) and World Bank EHS guidelines. To protect water resources, construction runoff will be routed through sedimentation basins or silt traps before discharge, and hazardous materials will be stored away from drainage channels. Sanitation facilities for workers will be installed to prevent contamination of nearby water bodies. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) measures form a central part of the mitigation strategy. Contractors must implement a site-specific Health and Safety Plan, supply appropriate PPE to all workers, conduct regular safety training, maintain first-aid facilities, and ensure availability of drinking water, sanitation, and rest areas. Emergency preparedness and incident reporting systems will be maintained to promote accountability and rapid response to any workplace incidents. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Furthermore, traffic and community safety will be managed through a site-specific Traffic Management Plan (TMP), including route scheduling for heavy vehicles, use of warning signage and flagmen, enforcement of speed limits, and coordination with local authorities and community representatives. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Collectively, these measures will ensure that construction activities for flood shelter development in Bogura District proceed safely, reduce environmental pollution, protect ecological and community health, and promote compliance with national regulations and World Bank safeguard standards, thereby contributing to long-term environmental resilience and community wellbeing. [SOURCE: Page_43]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 5     ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL MANAGEMENT PLAN (ESMP) 5.1       Purpose of the ESMP [SOURCE: Page_44]

The purpose of the Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) for the RIVER Project in Bogura District is to ensure that the flood shelter construction activities are planned, implemented, and monitored in full compliance with the Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) of the World Bank and the relevant environmental and social regulations of Bangladesh. The ESMP is a critical operational tool that identifies, assesses, and addresses potential environmental and social risks and impacts associated with the construction and future operation of 21 disaster-resilient flood shelters located in just Two upazilas—Gabtali (12 sites), and Shariakandi (9 sites). Given the sites in Bogura’s vulnerability to seasonal flooding, riverbank erosion, and waterlogging, the ESMP incorporates measures to minimize adverse environmental and social impacts while maximizing community resilience and adaptive capacity. It integrates site-specific mitigation measures, monitoring protocols, institutional responsibilities, capacity-building requirements, and grievance redress mechanisms to ensure sustainability and social inclusion throughout the project lifecycle. The ESMP particularly ensures that vulnerable groups—including women, children, elderly persons, persons with disabilities, and marginalized households—are not disproportionately affected and are able to benefit from the project’s outcomes. It promotes equitable access to shelter facilities during emergencies and ensures inclusive use during normal periods, such as for educational or community purposes. The Project Implementation Unit (PIU) of LGED will be responsible for the overall coordination, supervision, and enforcement of the ESMP. Contractors will be directly accountable for implementing mitigation measures during construction in strict adherence to both national environmental and labor laws and the World Bank Environmental and Social Standards (ESSs). 5.2       Access to Translated Information To ensure transparency, the Environmental and Social Assessment and Management Report and the ESMP will be disseminated locally within all six upazilas of Sirajganj District. Copies the documents will be distributed to:     Contractors’ site office     School authorities where shelters are being constructed     Relevant LGED field offices The final assessment report will be uploaded to the LGED official website and the World Bank website following formal approval, in compliance with ESS10: Stakeholder Engagement and Information Disclosure. [SOURCE: Page_44]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 5.3   Environmental and Social Management Plan The implementation of the school-cum-Flood Shelter along with connecting roads (where applicable) construction sub-project requires a comprehensive framework of preventive and management measures to ensure environmental and social sustainability throughout its life cycle. The Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) serves as the overarching tool that identifies site-specific risks, proposes mitigation actions, defines monitoring parameters, and assigns responsibilities to ensure that construction activities—including earthworks, access road improvement, tree removal, and installation of renewable features—comply with environmental and social safeguards. Complementing the ESMP, the Environmental and Social Codes of Practice (ESCOPs) provide detailed technical and procedural guidance for the contractor and field supervisors to manage recurring issues such as Waste Management, Water Resource Management, Drainage Management, Air Quality Management, and Construction Camp Management, etc. These ESCOPs standardize good practices across all sites, reducing the likelihood of non-compliance and promoting environmentally sound and socially responsible construction behavior. In parallel, the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for pile driving and building demolition address two high-risk activities that require specific operational control— ensuring noise, vibration, dust, and structural safety risks are minimized, and that occupational and community safety standards are strictly maintained. Together, the ESMP, ESCOPs, and SOPs form an integrated management system that links prevention, mitigation, and monitoring, ensuring that the project achieves its infrastructure objectives while safeguarding human health, local communities, and the surrounding environment. [SOURCE: Page_45]

The activity wise anticipated environmental and social impacts and corresponding mitigation measures and Site-Specific Impacts and mitigation/management measures have been outlined in Table 5.1 and Table 5.2. A detailed monitoring framework for overall ES Performance has been presented in Table 5.4. Additionally, Contractor must follow the Standard Operating Procedure delineated in Annex-6. [SOURCE: Page_45]

The ESMP ensures compliance with the World Bank’s ten Environmental and Social Standards (ESSs), particularly focusing on ESS$_1$ (Assessment and Management of Environmental and Social Risks and Impacts), ESS$_2$ (Labor and Working Conditions), ESS$_3$ (Resource Efficiency and Pollution Prevention), ESS$_4$ (Community Health and Safety), and ESS10 (Stakeholder Engagement and Information Disclosure). It provides guidelines for managing construction- related impacts such as air and water pollution, noise, occupational health and safety risks, and impacts on local livelihoods and ecosystems. [SOURCE: Page_45]

Moreover, the ESMP emphasizes the importance of stakeholder engagement, grievance redress mechanisms, and the inclusion of vulnerable groups to promote equitable and sustainable outcomes. By integrating environmental and social considerations into every stage of project implementation, the ESMP supports responsible infrastructure development that enhances community resilience while minimizing adverse impacts. [SOURCE: Page_45]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District 5.4   Monitoring of ES Performance [SOURCE: Page_56]

A robust monitoring system is essential to ensure that the preventive, management, and mitigation measures outlined in the ESMP, ESCOPs, and SOPs are effectively implemented during the construction and operational phases of the School-cum-Flood Shelter sub-project. Monitoring enables project authorities to track compliance, evaluate performance, and identify potential environmental and social risks at an early stage. [SOURCE: Page_56]

This monitoring plan defines the parameters to be monitored, frequency and timing, responsible parties, and verification methods for each key environmental and social aspect. It integrates site-level actions by contractors with oversight by the Project Implementation Unit (PIU), Design and Supervision Consultant (D&SC), and—where applicable—the Directorate of Primary Education (DPE) and the community. [SOURCE: Page_56]

Monitoring will be both proactive (preventive)—through inspections, audits, and consultations—and reactive (corrective)—based on incident reports, grievances, and non-compliance notices. The plan aligns with national environmental standards (DoE, Bangladesh), the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Framework (ESF), and LGED’s internal Environmental and Social Management Guidelines. [SOURCE: Page_56]

Table 5.3: Monitoring Framework for achieving overall ES Performance [SOURCE: Page_56]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District [SOURCE: Page_59]

5.5   Capacity Development Measures Effective management of Environmental, Social, and Gender issues in construction projects requires proactive capacity building for all actors involved — including the Implementing Agency, Contractors, and Supervision Consultants. To ensure compliance with environmental and social standards, all project stakeholders must be adequately trained and informed about their responsibilities, mitigation measures, and reporting mechanisms. Capacity-building programs — through formal trainings, on-site guidance, tool-box meetings, and awareness sessions — help strengthen institutional capacity, improve coordination, and ensure that sustainability and gender equity principles are integrated into project planning, implementation, and monitoring. The following table outlines the recommended capacity-building measures, target participants, training frequency, and key topics to be covered under an ESG management framework for building and road construction projects. 5.6   Cost of Environmental Enhancement Works in BOQ Considering the environmental impacts and their mitigation measures for this sub-project, several items are included in the Bill of Quantities (BOQ) to address these issues. The detailed site-specific estimate, with tentative cost for implementing the ESMP, is given in annexure 1. As per project ESMF, PIU, project engineer’s suggestion and experience from other LGED implemented projects, adequate budget has been proposed for the environmental management for the mitigation and enhancement measures. It may vary depending on the real time situation and requirement of the construction. An allocation for some environmental enhancement works such as tree plantation and Dust Suppression is included in the ESMP budget. Moreover, in order to ensure health safety and sanitary measures of workers by providing labor shed, PPEs, First Aid Box, drinking water facility, temporary but separate latrine for male and female workers as well as waste disposal systems, necessary budgetary allocation is provisioned. As the workforce at site need to be sensitized on environmental and social performance issues, motivational training on environmental and social considerations has been taken into account. The budget for labor shed, temporay school facility and site office construction is included in the civil works items. Therefore, these are not included in the environmental budget. It should be noted that the contractor will be paid as per actual work done. As there is no resettlement issue involved, no resettlement budget is required for land acquisition and compensation of any forms. 5.7   Environmental and Social Codes of Practice For the Flood Shelter Construction Project under the “Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER)” initiative in Sirajganj District, strict adherence to Environmental and Social Codes of Practice (ESCoPs) is essential to ensure sustainable and responsible implementation. These ESCoPs provide a standardized framework to minimize, mitigate, and manage potential environmental and social impacts associated with construction activities. The practices include site-specific measures such as proper waste management, noise and dust control, prevention of surface water contamination, and ensuring worker health and safety through the provision of personal protective equipment (PPE) and sanitation facilities. Social codes emphasize stakeholder engagement, avoiding disruption to local communities, protecting vulnerable groups, and ensuring no child labor or forced labor is used. During construction, care must be taken to avoid damage to existing infrastructure and natural habitats, while post- construction restoration of the site is mandatory. These codes also promote grievance redress mechanisms and compliance monitoring to uphold transparency and accountability throughout the project lifecycle. Effective implementation of ESCoPs not only ensures regulatory compliance and alignment with World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) standards but also contributes to the long-term resilience and acceptability of the flood shelter infrastructure in the local context of Bogura District. [SOURCE: Page_62]

Resilient Infrastructure for Adaptation and Vulnerability Reduction (RIVER) Project Environmental & Social Screening Report for Bogura District [SOURCE: Page_63]

The Contractor shall carry out the subproject related activities as specified in contract agreement. Environmental awareness creation, particularly about the direct construction impacts and for the health, pollution and safety issues will be Contractor’s responsibility. Details of the Environmental and Social Code of Practices (ESCoPs) are included in Annexure 5. 6     PUBLIC CONSULTATION MEETING 6.1    Stakeholder Engagement As part of the Environmental and Social Screening process for the Flood Shelter Construction Project (RIVER) in Bogura District, a comprehensive series of stakeholder engagement and site- specific consultation meetings were conducted at 20 proposed shelter sites. SMC of one proposed shelter was found disagreed to provide school ground for construction works, which for a replacement is required. However, all those consultation meetings were held from June 29, 2025 to July 5, 2025, covering various unions and villages where the flood shelters are planned. The objective of these consultations was to ensure the active participation of local stakeholders, including Union Parishad representatives, school management committees, teachers, local community members, female representatives, and vulnerable groups, in the project planning and decision-making process. During the meetings, detailed discussions were held on potential environmental and social impacts, site-specific concerns, benefits of the proposed shelters, and measures for ensuring inclusiveness and minimizing disruption during construction and operational phases. The feedback received from the stakeholders was constructive and has been duly incorporated into the Environmental and Social Management Plans (ESMPs). These engagements not only enhanced transparency and local ownership but also ensured that the site selection and design of flood shelters are contextually appropriate and socially accepted. Refer to Annexure 4 for details of the attendance of the meeting. 6.2    Methodology Site-specific consultation meetings were systematically conducted at 20 proposed flood shelter locations across Bogura District to ensure inclusive participation and transparent stakeholder engagement in accordance with the Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) prescribed ES Screening checklist and the project’s safeguard requirements. Environmental and Social Screening Checklist and Consultation checklist are attached in Annexure 2 and Annexure 3 respectively. The methodology followed a participatory and inclusive approach to engage with local communities, school management committees (SMC), Union Parishad representatives, teachers, farmers, women, and other vulnerable groups. Each meeting was organized at or near the shelter site, where project objectives, potential environmental and social impacts, and proposed mitigation measures were explained in simple, local language. Tools such as open discussions, focus group interactions, community mapping, and feedback collection were utilized to facilitate two-way communication. Attention was given to gender inclusion, with separate consultations or dedicated sessions to ensure women’s perspectives were adequately captured. [SOURCE: Page_63]
